You are researching a small dining district for a website. Four restaurants in downtown Danville, California (Contra Costa County, East Bay) sit on or around the same street corner at the south end of the Hartz Avenue downtown strip: Rancho Cantina, Incontro Ristorante, Kaia's Island Kitchen & Tiki Bar, and Harvest (Danville). The site will brand this as the "Danville Dining District" / "South of Hartz".
Tools: use WebSearch and WebFetch (load them with ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch" first). You may also use Bash with curl (e.g. curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0" URL | head -c 200000) to read pages that WebFetch cannot, and curl -sI to check headers. Never guess: every fact must come from a page you actually read. If something cannot be found, leave it empty and say so in notes. Do not invent hours, prices, or dishes.
Tasks: (1) Find the exact street address of each of the four and geocode each with Nominatim (https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search?q=<address>&format=json) or a maps link. (2) Identify the shared intersection/corner and its coordinates, and describe how the four relate physically (same block? across the street? distances in feet/minutes). (3) List nearby landmarks with coordinates: Village Theatre & Art Gallery, Iron Horse Regional Trail access, Danville Hotel/Prospect Ave area, Town Green/Oak Hill Park, Museum of the San Ramon Valley, Danville Library, Danville Farmers' Market location, Hartz Ave shopping, etc. (4) List public parking lots/garages in downtown Danville with addresses/coordinates and any time limits (the Town of Danville publishes a downtown parking map). (5) Describe the busier, younger nightlife cluster of restaurants/bars in Danville (where is it, which venues) so the site can position South of Hartz as the upscale alternative. (6) Summarize town facts useful for copy (population, character, downtown vibe, what closes early). Cite sources. Return only the structured object.

# Downtown Danville Parking Information

## Parking Lots Mentioned
The page specifically identifies two municipal parking lots where **employee permits are NOT valid**:
- Clocktower Municipal parking lot

## Permit Rules

**Eligibility & Verification:**
Applicants must provide "proof of employment either in the form of a recent pay stub or a business card," with verification completed online or at the Danville Police Department.

**Zone System:**
Three zones divide downtown parking. Zone 1 ("yellow") is accessible to all permit holders. Zones 2 ("red") and 3 ("blue") require employment "in the immediate vicinity" of your workplace.

**Pricing & Validity:**
- Zone 1: $25 annually
- Zones 2 & 3: $50 annually
- Permits are valid January 1–December 31

**Placement:**
Stickers must be "affixing it to the inside windshield on the lower left-hand side (driver's side)."

**Access Restrictions:**
"Employee permit parking is only valid in areas marked 'All Day Parking by Permit Only.'"

# Danville Hotel History

**Year Built:** 1892. The Contra Costa Gazette reported on November 3, 1892: "Danville can at last boast of a restaurant."

**Original Location & Address:** Edward and Mary Bridgett McCauley purchased lots 6-9 on Railroad Avenue for $500, positioned between Prospect Avenue and Short Street, across from the Southern Pacific station.

**Moves:** In 1927, the hotel and McCauley house were relocated to Hartz Avenue lots, facing east. This relocation reflected "the decreasing reliance on the train and increasing use of the automobile."

**Physical Description:** The original structure was a white-painted building with 18 rooms and a dining room accommodating 24 people, designed to serve train travelers and railroad workers.

**Today:** A new development called the "Danville Hotel" opened in 2016, featuring retail, restaurant, and residential spaces. The restored original Danville Hotel and McCauley House remain on the site.

**Street Descriptions:** 
- **Prospect Avenue & Short Street:** Defined the original hotel property boundaries
- **Railroad Avenue & Hartz Avenue:** As San Ramon Creek altered Front Street's utility, these avenues became the primary commercial corridors, with Hartz eventually becoming the main downtown thoroughfare

# Discover Danville Walking Tour Summary

**Description:**
An interactive, web-based app enabling visitors to create personalized walking tours featuring restaurants, shops, and historic landmarks throughout Danville. The tool provides historical context with archival photos and location-based navigation.

**URL:**
www.danville.ca.gov/DiscoverDanville

**Key Features:**
- Free access via mobile device; no downloads or logins needed
- Highlights Downtown Danville and surrounding areas
- Supports local businesses by directing foot traffic to small shops and restaurants

**Highlights Mentioned:**
- Historic landmarks spanning the town's 170-year history
- Local retail and dining establishments
- Early 1900s residential architecture (example: former home of Danville's first dentist)
- Downtown Danville storefronts and businesses

**Social Handles:**
The town maintains accounts on Facebook (@DanvilleCAgov), Twitter, Instagram (@danvillecagov), YouTube, LinkedIn, and Nextdoor, though none are specifically tagged in the article.

# Dining in Danville, CA

## Overview
The Town of Danville's official website features a comprehensive "Eat in Danville" directory listing over 150 dining establishments throughout the community.

## Key Dining Areas
The restaurant listings indicate significant concentrations along **Hartz Avenue** (the downtown corridor) and **Camino Tassajara**, with additional venues at **Crow Canyon Road** and **San Ramon Valley Boulevard**.

## Restaurant Categories
The directory encompasses diverse cuisines including:
- Sushi and Asian cuisine (Akira Sushi, Hashiya Sushi, Taru Japanese Cuisine)
- Mexican restaurants (Chronic Tacos, Diablo Taqueria, El Nido)
- Italian dining (Bridges, Taverna Sorrentina, Piatti)
- American fare (Black Bear Diner, Norm's Place, The Melt)
- Bakeries and cafes (Life is Sweet, Danville Old Towne Bakery)
- Breweries and bars (Danville Brewing Co., Canyon Club Brewery)
- International options (Lotus Thai, Falafel Boy, KavehG)

## Notable Establishments
Upscale dining venues include Forbes Mill Steakhouse, Locanda Ravello, and The Peasant & The Pear, alongside casual chains like Chipotle, Subway, and Starbucks.

The directory serves as a resource for residents and visitors exploring Danville's food and beverage scene.

## Overview
The Hartz House is a neoclassic rowhouse located at 455 Hartz Avenue in Danville, built circa 1910.

## Historical Significance
The home belonged to John Hartz, who was the town's first subdivider. John and Catharina Hartz owned 220 acres in Danville, stretching from behind the buildings on Front Street to the base of Las Trampas. They sold 8.5 acres to Southern Pacific for the railroad station, then subdivided the remainder into 74 lots. Thus, Hartz Avenue began.

## Original Use
The Hartz family lived in this house during retirement.

## Current Use
The building now houses Incontro Ristorante, offering upscale casual indoor dining in the historic Hartz House and romantic outdoor dining in a garden patio.

The Hartz House remains an important landmark in downtown Danville's historic district, and its preservation has allowed it to continue serving the community in a new capacity as a restaurant.

The Old Oak Tree is a Valley Oak located on Diablo Road, estimated to be over 350 years old and dating to circa 1600s. The tree is situated at the intersection area near Hartz Avenue in downtown Danville.

## Landmark Significance

The tree is a symbol for Danville, as well as its most notable landmark. The Danville Oak Tree has become a symbol of the community and, in many cases, a central point of meeting and communication in the Town.

## Structural Support

Estimated to be 350 years old, the Oak Tree has recently started to show its age. The tree was discovered to be in jeopardy of weakening and possibly falling down. With the support of the community, a special metal support structure was installed to prevent the tree from falling.

## Annual Celebration

Each year in November, the Town gathers on Diablo Road at the base of the tree to celebrate the annual Tree Lighting Ceremony. The longstanding tradition is a mainstay of the winter holiday season in Danville, held annually on the day after Thanksgiving.

The museum operates from a restored location and features exhibits, educational programs, and a permanent collection of artifacts related to local history.

# Danville Hotel Property Information

**Address:**
411 Hartz Avenue, Danville, CA

**Description:**
This mixed-use downtown development features "modern restaurant space, storefronts and second-floor residential units." The 2015 renovation preserved two heritage buildings—the McCauley House and Danville Hotel—officially recognized as town heritage resources by the local council.

**Current Tenants:**
The webpage does not list specific tenant names or businesses. While the property includes restaurant and retail spaces, no individual merchants or dining establishments are identified in this content.

**Leasing Contact:**
For space availability and tenant information, contact Jamie Lue at Castle Management (925-328-1240) or download the leasing brochure.

# Historical Narrative of Danville

## Founding
Danville was established by Daniel and Andrew Inman, who purchased 400 acres in 1854 using California Gold Rush earnings. By 1858, the settlement had developed basic commerce including a blacksmith, hotel, wheelwright, and general store. The community was named Danville in honor of Andrew's mother-in-law from Kentucky and the enterprising Daniel Inman.

## Post Office & Early Growth
"The Danville Post Office opened in 1860 with hotel owner Henry W Harris as the first postmaster." The 1869 census showed nearly 1,800 residents in the combined Danville-Lafayette areas. Settlers established ranches and farms, producing cattle, wheat, hay, fruit crops, walnuts, and almonds.

## Hartz Family & Avenue Development
John Hartz played a pivotal role in downtown transformation. He donated 8.65 acres for the railroad station and granted land access. Subsequently, "He then subdivided and sold lots east of the station, shifting the town's focus from Front Street to Hartz Avenue." The resulting commercial corridor included a bank, drug store, saloon, doctor's office, and Chinese laundry, with the Danville Hotel relocated to face Hartz Avenue in 1927.

## Railroad Impact (1891)
The Southern Pacific Railroad's arrival dramatically changed Danville, enabling efficient crop shipment and improved transportation, shifting the commercial center eastward from the original Front Street location.

The Town Green Pavilion is an outdoor performance venue located at the Danville Community Center and Danville Library. It serves as "a welcoming outdoor setting for concerts, performances, and community gatherings."

Danville Community Center and Danville Library, Danville, CA

input.walking_notes: All four sit within about 250 ft of each other around the Hartz Ave & Church St intersection (OSM intersection node 37.820604, -121.998233). Hartz Ave runs NW–SE through downtown; odd numbers (Incontro 455, Rancho 501) are on the southwest side, even numbers (Kaia's 480, Harvest 500) on the northeast side. Church St crosses Hartz here (running SW to Railroad Ave and NE toward Front St / Bridges). Layout by quadrant: Rancho Cantina occupies the corner building south of Church on the SW side (DanvilleSanRamon: 'southeast corner of Hartz Avenue and Church Street'); Danville Harvest is directly across Hartz from Rancho, south of Church on the NE side (about 120 ft / one crosswalk apart); Kaia's is on Harvest's side of Hartz, roughly 110 ft northwest of the intersection (across Church St from Harvest, ~160 ft door to door); Incontro is on Rancho's side, about 170 ft northwest of the intersection (across Church St from Rancho, ~220 ft; 485 Hartz/New Moon Massage sits between Incontro and the corner). Pairwise distances (building centroids): Rancho–Harvest ~120 ft, Kaia's–Harvest ~160 ft, Incontro–Kaia's ~155 ft, Rancho–Kaia's ~215 ft, Rancho–Incontro ~220 ft, Incontro–Harvest ~250 ft — every pairing is under a one-minute walk with at most one street crossing. The Hartz/Church intersection was the first phase (April 2024) of the Town's $4.9M Downtown Master Plan Catalyst Project, which added enhanced pedestrian crossings, traffic-calming bulb-outs and new lighting at five Hartz intersections from School St to Linda Mesa Ave, so the crossing between Rancho and Harvest is a rebuilt pedestrian crossing. Church St and School St are 2-hour street parking; Hartz Ave is mostly 2-hour with loading zones (Town parking map). Nearest lots: Village Theatre Municipal Lot ~340 ft NE via Church St; Front Street Municipal Lot ~420 ft; Railroad Ave Municipal Lot ~440 ft SW via Church St (backs onto the Iron Horse Trail, which passes ~40 ft from Railroad & Church). Upscale neighbors inside the same pocket: Bridges Restaurant & Bar at 44 Church St (~230 ft NE of the corner) and Crush'd Wine Bar + Kitchen at 312 Railroad Ave (~210 ft SW).
input.neighborhood_description: The four restaurants anchor the quieter southern end of Danville's historic Hartz Avenue, one block north of where Hartz meets San Ramon Valley Blvd/Hartz Way and a two-to-three-minute walk south of the busier Prospect Ave/Danville Hotel/Prospect Park Plaza core. This stretch is where Danville's late-1800s/early-1900s residences were converted into restaurants: Incontro occupies the c.1910 Hartz House (home of John Hartz, the subdivider who created Hartz Avenue), Harvest the c.1903 Eddy House, and further south sit the Cabral House (551), Bret Read House (571) and Shuey/Podva House (100 School St) from the Town's Historic Downtown Walking Tour. Bay Area Telegraph calls the Hartz/Church corner 'one of downtown Danville's busiest restaurant stretches'; the Town's Catalyst Project (2024–25) rebuilt the intersection with bulb-outs, enhanced crossings and new light poles/lit bollards. Within ~250 ft are Bridges Restaurant & Bar (44 Church St, the Mrs. Doubtfire restaurant) and Crush'd Wine Bar + Kitchen (312 Railroad Ave, 24 wines on tap); the Village Theatre & Art Gallery (233 Front St, the 1874 Grange Hall) is ~315 ft NE; the Iron Horse Trail and the Railroad Ave lot (Saturday Farmers' Market) are one short block SW via Church St. The Town's official 'Live Locally' branding, the oak-tree logo and the 350-year-old Old Oak Tree (Diablo Rd, ~980 ft NE) frame the local identity. Compared with the north-Hartz/Prospect block (dive bar, music club, piano bar, brewery), this pocket is dinner-and-patio oriented: wood-fired Californio Mexican (Rancho, opened Aug 24, 2026), regional Italian in a historic house (Incontro, closed Mondays), farm-to-table (Harvest, dinner ends 8:30 pm daily) and Hawaiian/tiki cocktails with live Hawaiian music (Kaia's, bar to 11 pm Fri–Sat). Hours as read Sept 10, 2026 — Rancho Sun–Thu 11–10, Fri–Sat 11–11; Incontro dinner Tue–Thu & Sun 5–9, Fri–Sat 5–10, brunch buffet Sat 12–3 / Sun 10–2; Kaia's Sun–Tue 11:30–9, Wed–Thu 11:30–10, Fri–Sat 11:30–11 (kitchen closes an hour before the bar); Harvest lunch weekdays 11:30–3, brunch weekends 10–3, dinner daily 4–8:30, happy hour 3–5.

input.town_facts: Town of Danville, Contra Costa County (East Bay), 'Heart of the San Ramon Valley'; ~30 miles east of San Francisco. Population 43,582 (2020 Census, Wikipedia) / 'approximately 43,146' (Town Community Profile); 18 sq mi; incorporated July 1, 1982 and one of the few California municipalities styled 'Town'. Founded 1854 by brothers Daniel and Andrew Inman on 400 acres bought with Gold Rush earnings; named Danville by 1858; post office 1860. The Southern Pacific branch line arrived June 7, 1891; John Hartz gave/sold 8.65 acres for the depot and subdivided 74 lots east of it, shifting commerce from Front St to the new Hartz Avenue; the Danville Hotel was turned to face Hartz in 1927. Wealthy, family-oriented suburb: Wikipedia cites ZIP 94506 as the 14th-wealthiest in America and the town as 2nd-highest-income U.S. place with 40,000+ residents. SafeWise named Danville California's safest city for 2026 (No. 1 six of the past nine years; violent crime 0.6 and property crime 5.9 per 1,000) — Town news release Feb 12, 2026. Town copy describes 'the perfect blend of upscale amenities and small-town charm', a 'quaint character', highly rated schools, year-round farmers' markets and street fairs, and a historic downtown of shops, restaurants and galleries 'from upscale eateries to family-friendly pizzerias'. Official brand since 2017: 'Live Locally' with an oak-tree logo (#LiveLocallyDanville); the 350-year-old Old Oak Tree on Diablo Rd is the town symbol and mascot Auggie the Acorn's home. Downtown investment: $4.9M Downtown Master Plan Catalyst Project (begun April 2024 at Hartz & Church) rebuilt five Hartz intersections from School St to Linda Mesa with raised/bulb-out crossings, lit bollards and new light poles; Prospect Park Plaza reopened July 2025 with a stage and oak sculptures; a new Town Green Pavilion starts construction Aug 2026 (done Spring 2027). What closes early (as read Sept 10, 2026): Museum of the SRV by 4 pm; Danville Harvest dinner ends 8:30 pm daily; Bridges dinner ends 8 pm Sun–Thu / 9 pm Fri–Sat; Danville Brewing bar 9 pm (9:30 Fri–Sat); Incontro 9 pm Tue–Thu & Sun, 10 pm Fri–Sat (closed Mondays); Crush'd 9 pm (10 Thu–Sat); Kaia's 9 pm Sun–Tue, 10 Wed–Thu, 11 Fri–Sat; Rancho Cantina 10 pm (11 Fri–Sat); Revel and Norm's 10–11 pm; Auburn Lounge is the late option at midnight nightly. The two 1-am venues (Kick N Mule, Stilettos) are listed closed. Farmers' Market Saturdays 9–1; Town offices M–Th 8–5, F 8–1. Downtown parking is free (1,400+ public spaces, six municipal lots), which the Town and press consistently highlight.

data.walking_notes: All four sit within about 250 ft of each other around the Hartz Ave & Church St intersection (OSM intersection node 37.820604, -121.998233). Hartz Ave runs NW–SE through downtown; odd numbers (Incontro 455, Rancho 501) are on the southwest side, even numbers (Kaia's 480, Harvest 500) on the northeast side. Church St crosses Hartz here (running SW to Railroad Ave and NE toward Front St / Bridges). Layout by quadrant: Rancho Cantina occupies the corner building south of Church on the SW side (DanvilleSanRamon: 'southeast corner of Hartz Avenue and Church Street'); Danville Harvest is directly across Hartz from Rancho, south of Church on the NE side (about 120 ft / one crosswalk apart); Kaia's is on Harvest's side of Hartz, roughly 110 ft northwest of the intersection (across Church St from Harvest, ~160 ft door to door); Incontro is on Rancho's side, about 170 ft northwest of the intersection (across Church St from Rancho, ~220 ft; 485 Hartz/New Moon Massage sits between Incontro and the corner). Pairwise distances (building centroids): Rancho–Harvest ~120 ft, Kaia's–Harvest ~160 ft, Incontro–Kaia's ~155 ft, Rancho–Kaia's ~215 ft, Rancho–Incontro ~220 ft, Incontro–Harvest ~250 ft — every pairing is under a one-minute walk with at most one street crossing. The Hartz/Church intersection was the first phase (April 2024) of the Town's $4.9M Downtown Master Plan Catalyst Project, which added enhanced pedestrian crossings, traffic-calming bulb-outs and new lighting at five Hartz intersections from School St to Linda Mesa Ave, so the crossing between Rancho and Harvest is a rebuilt pedestrian crossing. Church St and School St are 2-hour street parking; Hartz Ave is mostly 2-hour with loading zones (Town parking map). Nearest lots: Village Theatre Municipal Lot ~340 ft NE via Church St; Front Street Municipal Lot ~420 ft; Railroad Ave Municipal Lot ~440 ft SW via Church St (backs onto the Iron Horse Trail, which passes ~40 ft from Railroad & Church). Upscale neighbors inside the same pocket: Bridges Restaurant & Bar at 44 Church St (~230 ft NE of the corner) and Crush'd Wine Bar + Kitchen at 312 Railroad Ave (~210 ft SW).
data.neighborhood_description: The four restaurants anchor the quieter southern end of Danville's historic Hartz Avenue, one block north of where Hartz meets San Ramon Valley Blvd/Hartz Way and a two-to-three-minute walk south of the busier Prospect Ave/Danville Hotel/Prospect Park Plaza core. This stretch is where Danville's late-1800s/early-1900s residences were converted into restaurants: Incontro occupies the c.1910 Hartz House (home of John Hartz, the subdivider who created Hartz Avenue), Harvest the c.1903 Eddy House, and further south sit the Cabral House (551), Bret Read House (571) and Shuey/Podva House (100 School St) from the Town's Historic Downtown Walking Tour. Bay Area Telegraph calls the Hartz/Church corner 'one of downtown Danville's busiest restaurant stretches'; the Town's Catalyst Project (2024–25) rebuilt the intersection with bulb-outs, enhanced crossings and new light poles/lit bollards. Within ~250 ft are Bridges Restaurant & Bar (44 Church St, the Mrs. Doubtfire restaurant) and Crush'd Wine Bar + Kitchen (312 Railroad Ave, 24 wines on tap); the Village Theatre & Art Gallery (233 Front St, the 1874 Grange Hall) is ~315 ft NE; the Iron Horse Trail and the Railroad Ave lot (Saturday Farmers' Market) are one short block SW via Church St. The Town's official 'Live Locally' branding, the oak-tree logo and the 350-year-old Old Oak Tree (Diablo Rd, ~980 ft NE) frame the local identity. Compared with the north-Hartz/Prospect block (dive bar, music club, piano bar, brewery), this pocket is dinner-and-patio oriented: wood-fired Californio Mexican (Rancho, opened Aug 24, 2026), regional Italian in a historic house (Incontro, closed Mondays), farm-to-table (Harvest, dinner ends 8:30 pm daily) and Hawaiian/tiki cocktails with live Hawaiian music (Kaia's, bar to 11 pm Fri–Sat). Hours as read Sept 10, 2026 — Rancho Sun–Thu 11–10, Fri–Sat 11–11; Incontro dinner Tue–Thu & Sun 5–9, Fri–Sat 5–10, brunch buffet Sat 12–3 / Sun 10–2; Kaia's Sun–Tue 11:30–9, Wed–Thu 11:30–10, Fri–Sat 11:30–11 (kitchen closes an hour before the bar); Harvest lunch weekdays 11:30–3, brunch weekends 10–3, dinner daily 4–8:30, happy hour 3–5.

Town-owned theater + art gallery (gallery hours Wed–Fri 12–5, Sat 11–3 per Town page; offices M–Th 8–5, F 8–1). ~315 ft / 1–2 min NE of the corner via Church St. Adjacent Village Theatre Municipal Lot has 2-hr and 4-hr sections with EV charging.

Castle Companies' 2015–16 redevelopment preserved the hotel and McCauley House (dedicated town heritage resources 2016) and added ~35,000–37,500 sq ft of retail/restaurant space plus 16 second-floor residences at Hartz & W Prospect. ~380 ft / 1–2 min NW of the corner.

data.town_facts: Town of Danville, Contra Costa County (East Bay), 'Heart of the San Ramon Valley'; ~30 miles east of San Francisco. Population 43,582 (2020 Census, Wikipedia) / 'approximately 43,146' (Town Community Profile); 18 sq mi; incorporated July 1, 1982 and one of the few California municipalities styled 'Town'. Founded 1854 by brothers Daniel and Andrew Inman on 400 acres bought with Gold Rush earnings; named Danville by 1858; post office 1860. The Southern Pacific branch line arrived June 7, 1891; John Hartz gave/sold 8.65 acres for the depot and subdivided 74 lots east of it, shifting commerce from Front St to the new Hartz Avenue; the Danville Hotel was turned to face Hartz in 1927. Wealthy, family-oriented suburb: Wikipedia cites ZIP 94506 as the 14th-wealthiest in America and the town as 2nd-highest-income U.S. place with 40,000+ residents. SafeWise named Danville California's safest city for 2026 (No. 1 six of the past nine years; violent crime 0.6 and property crime 5.9 per 1,000) — Town news release Feb 12, 2026. Town copy describes 'the perfect blend of upscale amenities and small-town charm', a 'quaint character', highly rated schools, year-round farmers' markets and street fairs, and a historic downtown of shops, restaurants and galleries 'from upscale eateries to family-friendly pizzerias'. Official brand since 2017: 'Live Locally' with an oak-tree logo (#LiveLocallyDanville); the 350-year-old Old Oak Tree on Diablo Rd is the town symbol and mascot Auggie the Acorn's home. Downtown investment: $4.9M Downtown Master Plan Catalyst Project (begun April 2024 at Hartz & Church) rebuilt five Hartz intersections from School St to Linda Mesa with raised/bulb-out crossings, lit bollards and new light poles; Prospect Park Plaza reopened July 2025 with a stage and oak sculptures; a new Town Green Pavilion starts construction Aug 2026 (done Spring 2027). What closes early (as read Sept 10, 2026): Museum of the SRV by 4 pm; Danville Harvest dinner ends 8:30 pm daily; Bridges dinner ends 8 pm Sun–Thu / 9 pm Fri–Sat; Danville Brewing bar 9 pm (9:30 Fri–Sat); Incontro 9 pm Tue–Thu & Sun, 10 pm Fri–Sat (closed Mondays); Crush'd 9 pm (10 Thu–Sat); Kaia's 9 pm Sun–Tue, 10 Wed–Thu, 11 Fri–Sat; Rancho Cantina 10 pm (11 Fri–Sat); Revel and Norm's 10–11 pm; Auburn Lounge is the late option at midnight nightly. The two 1-am venues (Kick N Mule, Stilettos) are listed closed. Farmers' Market Saturdays 9–1; Town offices M–Th 8–5, F 8–1. Downtown parking is free (1,400+ public spaces, six municipal lots), which the Town and press consistently highlight.

data.notes: Scope and caveats: (1) Coordinates are OpenStreetMap building/POI centroids retrieved via Overpass and Nominatim on Sept 10, 2026 (±10–20 m); the corner coordinate is the actual OSM street-intersection node of Hartz Ave and Church St. Distances are straight-line haversine values, so real walking paths are slightly longer. (2) Addresses were read from each restaurant's own website (ranchocantina.com/danville, incontrodanville.com, kaiasdanville.com, danvilleharvest.com/contact). Rancho Cantina's phone on its site is (925) 718-5153; a search summary showed (925) 519-3851 — use the site's. Rancho's soft-open date: Bay Area Telegraph says Monday Aug 24, 2026 (reservations Sep 1); Diablo Dish says 'Monday, August 26' (Aug 26, 2026 is a Wednesday, so likely a typo). (3) Hours are as read on Sept 10, 2026 and should be re-verified before publishing. (4) Parking time limits were read visually from the Town's color-coded Downtown Public Parking Map PDF (DocumentCenter/View/2427): orange = 3 hr (Clock Tower, Front Street, Rose Street), blue = 4 hr (Library/CC; parts of Village Theatre and Railroad lots), green = 2 hr (parts of Village Theatre and Railroad lots; most streets), dark green = 72 hr (Sycamore Valley Park & Ride). Lot capacities are not published except OSM's 82 for the Library lot. Sycamore Valley Park & Ride was not geocoded. (5) Village Theatre history (1874 Grange Hall) is from the Town's Historic Downtown Walking Tour Guide PDF; a search snippet of a Town page said 1873 and a 1,000 sq ft gallery opened Nov 14, 2009 — that page's text was not read directly. (6) Nightlife closures: Kick N Mule (340 Hartz) and Stilettos Piano Bar (148 E Prospect, ex-McGah's) appear as 'CLOSED' in Yelp listing titles surfaced by search (Feb and Aug 2026 respectively) and stilettosdanville.com does not resolve; no replacement tenant was found for 340 Hartz. Treat both as closed-pending-verification. (7) Not found / empty: 2026 dates for Lighting of the Old Oak Tree, Oktoberfest Danville and Danville Fallfest (the Chamber's Oct 2026 calendar shows neither Oktoberfest nor Fallfest; danvillefallfest.com is parked). 'Evenings in Danville' and discoverdowntowndanville.org in search results belong to Danville, INDIANA — excluded. (8) EBParks Iron Horse page and SFGate's Hartz Ave article returned 403/blank; Instagram profiles could not be read, so @discoverdanville ownership and @eastbayeats follower count are unverified; #LiveLocallyDanville is confirmed via the Town's 2017 Nextdoor branding post and LinkedIn. (9) The Danville Hotel's current tenants are not listed on the owner's page; OSM shows Basque Boulangerie Café there (unverified). (10) Oak Hill Park is ~1.6 mi north of downtown — not a walkable landmark for the district. (11) No prices or dishes were recorded beyond concept descriptions quoted from the restaurants' own sites and press.
